(1)

In the Supreme Court of the United States


No. 25-5930

WILLIAM MAXWELL , PETITIONER

v.

SANDRA DINIS, ACTING WARDEN


ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE FIFTH CIRCUIT


REPLY BRIEF FOR THE PETITIONER


The court of appeals held in this case that habeas is
unavailable unless a prisoner seeks outright release from
custody.  The government agrees with Mr. Maxwell that
the decision below is incorrect  and should be vacated.
Even the amicus appointed to defend the judgment below
does not defend the Fifth Circuit’s rule.  Amicus accepts
that at least some level-of-custody claims are cognizable
in habeas, but argues that Mr. Maxwell’s claim is not
among them.  Amicus can def end the court of appeals’
judgment only by abandoning its reasoning and substituting an entirely new approach in its place.
But amicus’s approach is barely better.  Amicus proposes to limit habeas to thr ee newly discovered categories—an arbitrary taxonomy that finds no footing in the
text of the habeas statute, the history of habeas, or the

2

reasoning of this Court’s precedents.  Instead, amicus
simply gathers the facts of the cases this Court has already decided and declares the set closed without explaining why.  Amicus also endeavors to back into his preferred
result, arguing that Mr. Maxwell ’s claim is a conditionsof-confinement claim and theref ore not cognizable in habeas.  But while some cases have held that claims that fall
at the core of habeas cannot be brought under Section
1983, amicus cites no authority for using a conditions-ofconfinement label to remove from habeas a type of challenge that otherwise would fa ll within it.  And Mr. Maxwell’s claim is not a conditions-of-confinement claim at all:
he contends that continued co nfinement in prison, whatever the conditions, is unlawful.
Amicus also suggests that Mr. Maxwell is not seeking
to change his level of custody.  Amicus seizes on Congress’s reference to individual s on prerelease custody as
“prisoners” to argue that halfway houses and home confinement are simply a form of prison.  But the relevant
statutes make clear that prer elease custody is a distinct
form of “custody,” which is the relevant inquiry here, and
Congress has repeatedly di stinguished halfway houses
and home confinement from pr ison in other provisions.
Amicus’s effort to answer the fact that Mr. Maxwell’s
claim involves a change in custodian likewise overlooks
that the relevant custodian for purposes of habeas is not
the broader agency but rather the person with immediate
custody over the prisoner.  Amicus next relies on a few
cherry-picked anecdotes describing prison camps, while
disregarding the robust body of case law and other evidence recognizing that prerelease custody is materially
less restrictive than prison.  And he fails to appreciate that
prerelease custody is much more analogous to parole than
is his preferred alternative of supervised release.

3

Finally, although the gove rnment agrees that the decision below is incorrect and that the judgment should be
vacated, it tosses out two alternative theories for why Mr.
Maxwell’s habeas claim might ultimately fail.  As the government itself promptly reco gnizes, this Court’s normal
practice would be to leave arguments of that sort for consideration on remand.  On  the merits, the government’s
argument about administrative exhaustion is no more
persuasive than it was when the government raised it in
its brief in opposition.  And its argument about the judicial
review bar in 18 U.S.C. 3621(b)—which the government
did not raise in the court of appeals or at the certiorari
stage—overlooks the fact that the bar applies to claims
“under this subsection” rather than the distinct subsections (18 U.S.C. 3624(g), 3632(d)(4)) that required Mr.
Maxwell’s release to a half way house or home confinement on the basis of earned-time credits.  The government also raises the possibilit y that it might release Mr.
Maxwell within a few months, mooting this case; but even
if it does so before this Court issues its opinion, Mr. Maxwell’s claim will remain live.  This Court should reverse
the judgment below and remand for consideration of the
merits of Mr. Maxwell’s claim.*
A. A Claim Seeking To Change The Level Of Custody Is
Cognizable In Habeas
Despite being appointed to  defend the judgment below, amicus is not able to offer any argument supporting
the rule adopted by the court of appeals.  Instead, amicus
concedes that level-of-custody claims can be actionable.

* Although this case does not concern the underlying criminal prosecution, Mr. Maxwell disputes the government’s and amicus’s characterization of his alleged conduct as explained in his pending motion
under 28 U.S.C. 2255.  See Maxwell v. United States , Civ. No. 25-
16419, Dkt. 6 (D.N.J. Jan. 12, 2026).

4

See Br. 25-26 (citing Skinner v. Switzer, 562 U.S. 521, 534
(2011)).  But he attempts to resuscitate the judgment below by arguing that only certain level-of-custody claims
are cognizable, while all others are not.  Id. at 20, 25.  By
all appearances, amicus seeks to confine habeas jurisdiction to the precise examples previously recognized by this
Court’s precedents.  But he identifies no principle for distinguishing between level-of-custody claims that are in
and out, nor any coherent basi s for the Court’s decisions
to date.  Amicus’s other doctrinal move—contending that
claims of the type at issue he re are not cognizable in habeas because they are conditions-of-confinement claims—
likewise fails both in principle and in application.
1. Amicus’s proposed rule would limit habeas to
where: (1) the claim “implies that [the prisoner’s] physical
detention must be shortened or terminated”; (2) the claim
seeks “earlier release on bail  or parole”; or (3) the claim
contends that “the sentencing court ordered [the prisoner] to serve his sentence in a place it did not have jurisdiction to send him.”  Br. 20.  Amicus spends little time
justifying those categories (see id. at 21-23), and one
would search his brief in vain for any effort to ground
them in the text of the habeas statute or historical practice.
As an initial matter, am icus offers no reason why habeas should be limited to his proposed categories.  The
text of the habeas statute extends the writ to any prisoner
“in custody” in violation of federal law, and it broadly authorizes federal courts to “d ispose of the matter as law
and justice require.”  28 U.S.C. 2241, 2243; see Pet. Br. 16-
19.  History and precedent confirm that the writ has long
been used for any claims seeking release to a lower level
of custody.  See Pet. Br. 19-25; Habeas Scholars Br. 15-
29.  Amicus cannot identify a single authority that has purported to limit habeas to the categories he now identifies.

5

Remarkably, despite drawing his categories to accommodate precedent, amicus fails to account for one of this
Court’s most recent habeas decisions, Trump v. J.G.G.,
604 U.S. 670 (2025) (per curiam), which held that claims
challenging immigration removals fall within the scope of
habeas even if the detainees do not “formally request release from confinement.”  Id. at 672; see id. at 674 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring); Pet. Br. 28-29.  The immigration
transfers at issue in J.G.G. do not fit into any of amicus’s
categories: the detainees did not contest the fact of physical detention or the validity of a judgment or sentence,
nor seek release to bail or parole, nor challenge a court’s
order directing transfer that the court lacked jurisdiction
to direct.  Amicus’s approach  to habeas would therefore
have required the opposite result in J.G.G.
Nor do amicus’s three categories otherwise hold up.
As to the first, amicus suggests (Br. 21-22) that the province of habeas is seeking the invalidation of a judgment or
sentence.  But as this Court ha s made clear, the reach of
the writ is not so limited.  Instead, after the enactment of
28 U.S.C. 2255, Section 2241’s core function is providing a
vehicle for a prisoner to challenge “ ‘the legality of his detention’ without attacking the validity of his sentence.”
Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S. 465, 475 (2023)  (quoting 28
U.S.C. 2255(e)).
As to the second category, see Br. 22-23, 25, amicus
accepts that claims seeking earli er release on bail or parole are cognizable in habeas under this Court’s decisions,
but endeavors to limit those decisions to their facts.  The
decisions themselves forecl ose that approach.  Rather
than being limited to parole as amicus contends (Br. 25),
Preiser makes clear that habeas extends to claims in
which the petitioner is “being unlawfully subjected to
physical restraint” and seeks “release from such confinement,” including claims that a petitioner is “unlawfully

6

confined in the wrong institution.”  Preiser v. Rodriguez,
411 U.S. 475, 486 (1973); see Pet. Br. 25-26; U.S. Br. 21-
23.
Amicus also dismisses (Br. 25-26) this Court’s decision
in Skinner and Justice Scalia’s concurrence in Wilkinson,
which explained that habeas can be an available remedy
in cases in which “the relief sought would  *   *   *  ‘reduc[e] the level of custody.’ ”  562 U.S. at 534 (quoting Wilkinson v. Dotson, 544 U.S. 74, 86 (2005) (Scalia, J., concurring)); see Pet. Br. 26-27; U.S. Br. 23-24.  According to
amicus, that language is “best understood to apply to parole, bond, and [s]upervised [r]elease, not [p]rerelease
[c]ustody.”  Br. 25.  But that is not what the Court and
Justice Scalia actually said.
Amicus speculates that Just ice Scalia may have believed that level-of-custody claims are limited to “release
from incarceration to parole” based on the lower court authority cited in his opinion.  Br. 26.  But even accepting
that dubious premise, the unde rlying authority is not so
cramped.  In Graham v. Broglin, 922 F.2d 379 (1991), the
Seventh Circuit reasoned that the “general[]” rule is that
claims seeking a “quantum change in the level of custody”
are cognizable in habeas.  Id. at 381.  Amicus also points
(Br. 26) to a Third Circuit case cited in Graham (but not
by Justice Scalia), which rejected a habeas claim challenging the denial of a home furlough.  Wright v. Cuyler, 624
F.2d 455, 458 (1980).  But that decision hinged on the temporary nature of the furlough in question, which allowed
the prisoner to be released fo r seven days at a time, returning to prison at the end of that period.  Ibid.
Similarly, in defining his third category, amicus tries
to circumscribe this Court’s decision in Bonner as one
where the sentencing court lacked jurisdiction to send the
prisoner to a particular place.  Br. 23.  But the Court recognized in Bonner that habeas applies to restrictions on

7

liberty “from any source”—“equally as well from the unauthorized acts of courts a nd judges as the unauthorized
acts of individuals.”  151 U.S. 242, 259 (1894).  That easily
encompasses cases where the Executive violates the law
by keeping a person imprisoned in a place unauthorized
by statute.  Similarly, and contrary to amicus’s contention
(Br. 24, 27), Mr. Maxwell does claim that he is being detained in a “manner not authorized by his sentence” when
his sentence is properly viewed  in light of the First Step
Act, Hendrix, 599 U.S. at 475; see U.S. Br. 24.
2. Amicus also contends tha t the claim here is a conditions-of-confinement claim, which in amicus’s view
should take it outside the scop e of habeas.  Br. 16-20, 34-
37.  That argument fails at each turn.
As amicus acknowledges (Br. 16-17), this Court has
not resolved whether a condi tions-of-confinement claim
may ever be brought in habeas, see, e.g., Ziglar v. Abbasi,
582 U.S. 120, 144-145 (2017), and courts of appeals have
long been divided on the issue, see, e.g., Fortner v.
Eischen, 170 F.4th 655, 656 (8th Cir. 2026).  This case
would be a poor vehicle to resolve that conflict, given that
it involves a federal prisoner and federal and state prisoners may be differently situa ted with respect to whether
conditions-of-confinement claims are cognizable in habeas.  See Nettles v. Grounds, 830 F.3d 922, 931 & n.6 (9th
Cir. 2016) (en banc).
What is more, amicus’s conditions-of-confinementbased reasoning gets the analysis backwards.  This Court
has considered whether a claim falls within the core of habeas because civil-rights statutes contain an “implicit exception” for such claims in li ght of “considerations of linguistic specificity, history, and comity” that justify giving
the habeas statute precedence.  Wilkinson, 544 U.S. at 79.
Amicus cites no authority from this Court for the analytically inverse approach of first determining that a claim is

8

a conditions-of-confinement claim and then using that label to limit the scope of the habeas statute.
In any event, the argument fails on its own terms because amicus is wrong to trea t Mr. Maxwell’s First Step
Act claim as challenging his conditions of confinement.
See Br. 20, 29.  Mr. Maxwell does not seek better conditions within his existing custody.  No alteration of the “circumstances” of Mr. Maxwell’s incarceration would redress his claim here, see Muhammad v. Close, 540 U.S.
749, 750 (2004); Pet. Br. 38; in stead, the only remedy he
seeks is release from his present incarceration.  Amicus
offers no meaningful response to that central distinction.
Relatedly, amicus is wrong to suggest that Mr. Maxwell’s rule conflicts with decisions from this Court that
considered the merits of Section 1983 claims challenging
the transfer of prisoners to a maximum-security prison
and disciplinary confinement.   See Amicus Br. 35 (citing
Meachum v. Fano , 427 U.S. 215 (1976), and Haines v.
Kerner, 404 U.S. 519 (1972) (per curiam)).  Neither decision addressed the question whether Section 1983 rather
than habeas was the appropria te vehicle, and so those
cases do not “constitute precedents” for the scope-of-habeas question.  Cooper Industries, Inc. v. Aviall Services,
Inc., 543 U.S. 157, 170 (2004) (citation omitted).  In any
event, those decisions involv ed the discretionary movement among prisons “within the normal limits or range of
custody” authorized by the conviction, Meachum, 427
U.S. at 225-227, or within a single prison, see Haines, 404
U.S. at 519-520.  Mr. Maxwell’s claim, by contrast, is that
he is being imprisoned in a place “expressly forbidden” by
statute, which requires release to a distinct and materially
lower level of custody.  Bonner, 151 U.S. at 256.  Deeming
that claim cognizable would not resolve the availability of
habeas in the distinct scenarios amicus posits.

9

B. Mr. Maxwell’s Claim Seeking Accelerated Transfer To
A Halfway House Or To Home Confinement Challenges His Level Of Custody
Mr. Maxwell’s First Step Act claim seeking release to
a halfway house or home confinement is a level-of-custody
challenge for several reasons.  Federal law treats prerelease custody as a legally distinct form of custody; Mr.
Maxwell challenges his imme diate custodian’s authority
to hold him in prison; prerelease custody is materially less
restrictive than prison; and prerelease custody is analogous to parole in relevant respects.  See Pet. Br. 34-37;
U.S. Br. 25-32.  Because all those features point toward
the same conclusion, this Court need not resolve whether
any one standing alone suffices to create a cognizable custody claim.  See U.S. Br. 26.
1. To begin with, Congress established prerelease
custody as a legally distinct form of “custody.”  E.g., 18
U.S.C. 3624(g)(2), (4)-(5); see Pet. Br. 34.  Amicus does not
grapple with those statutory provisions and instead relies
solely on the fact that Section 3624 refers to those on prerelease custody as “prisone rs” whose term of imprisonment has not yet expired.  Br. 29 (citation omitted).  But
Congress’s use of the “prisone r[]” label is immaterial.
The question is whether prerelease custody is a distinct
form of “custody,” not whether it can, for some purposes,
be considered imprisonment.  28 U.S.C. 2241(c).  Moreover, far from viewing prerel ease custody and imprisonment as equivalent, Congress distinguished prisons and
community-based facilities in several provisions.  See U.S.
Br. 29-30 (citing provisions).  As the government explains,
the relevant statutes “make cl ear” that serving time on
“prerelease custody” is not the same as serving time in
“prison.”  Id. at 29.
Amicus’s argument on this poin t is also internally inconsistent.  Federal law calls those on supervised release

10

or on parole “prisoners,” even though amicus accepts that
a claim seeking supervised release or parole sounds in habeas.  See, e.g., 18 U.S.C. 1761(a), 3621(h)(5)(C)(iv), 4042(b).
And while amicus emphasizes that individuals released to
prerelease custody continue to serve their term of imprisonment, see Amicus Br. 29, so do individuals released on
parole, see Johnson v. United States, 529 U.S. 694, 725-
726 (2000) (Scalia, J., dissenting); Anderson v. Corall, 263
U.S. 193, 196 (1923).
2. Reinforcing the point, a First Step Act claim such
as the one at issue here seeks release from the unlawful
custody of the prison warden into the custody of another—generally, a resident ial reentry management officer.  See Pet. Br. 35.  That accords with the traditional
understanding of habeas, which “contemplate[s] a proceeding against some person who has the immediate custody of the party detained.”  Rumsfeld v. Padilla, 542 U.S.
426, 435 (2004) (quoting Wales v. Whitney, 114 U.S. 564,
574 (1885)).  That rule asks habeas’s fundamental question:  does the custodian have lawful power over this body
in this place?  See id. at 434-435.
Once again, amicus ignores that authority and instead
tries to move up a level of generality by noting that Mr.
Maxwell would still be within the custody of the Bureau of
Prisons on prerelease custody.  See Amicus Br. 23-24, 38-
39.  But that asks the wrong question:  a habeas claim
challenging present physical confinement operates
against the “immediate custodian,” not some “remote supervisory official”—let alone the broader agency.  Padilla, 542 U.S. at 435.  Indeed, if amicus’s agency-level reframing were correct, it is hard to justify amicus’s concession (and Preiser’s holding) that claims seeking release on
parole are cognizable in habeas given that both the Bureau of Prisons and the U. S. Parole Commission are
housed within the Department of Justice.  Cf. Amicus Br.

11

22-23.  As the government explains, the Bureau of Prisons’
“legal custody over someone in  prerelease custody is important for various purposes,” but “the availability of habeas is not one of them.”  Br. 29.
3. Prerelease custody is a lso materially less restrictive than prison, placing individuals in their own communities and allowing them much broader leeway to work,
attend religious services, and reconnect with their families, among other privileges.  See Pet. Br. 35-36; U.S. Br.
30-32; Raskin Br. 16.  Both longstanding case law and the
real-life experiences of those who have served time in a
halfway house or on home confinement confirm that prerelease custody is “not merely a change of address, but a
change in kind” from prison.  FAMM Br. 2, 11-18; see Pet.
Br. 36 (collecting cases).  That makes sense given that the
core purpose of prerelease c ustody is to help prisoners
prepare for reentry into the community.  See, e.g., 18
U.S.C. 3624(g)(2)(A)(i)(II)(gg), (g)(4).
Amicus ignores those authorities and instead relies on
a few anecdotal accounts to claim that some forms of incarceration may sometimes in volve similar conditions as
prerelease custody.  See Br. 6-9, 36-37.  But that misses
the point.  Even if the conditions in a prison camp may
sometimes look similar to the conditions in prerelease custody, that does not mean that serving time in prison is the
same as serving time in prerelease custody.  Under the
former, as amicus himself no tes, the Bureau of Prisons
has unreviewable authority to  assign a prisoner to a
higher-security facility.  See 18 U.S.C. 3621(b); Amicus
Br. 4-5.  Under the latter, by contrast, the prisoner has a
“statutory entitlement” (U.S. Br. 25) to less restrictive
conditions, which grow “increasingly less restrictive” over
time.  18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(4).  The meaningful measure is
the ceiling on restraint, not a temporary status that can
be taken away at any time.  And while amicus cites (Br.

12

37) a single decision for the notion that a halfway house is
a sort of “twilight zone between prison and freedom,” that
decision agreed with the Bureau of Prisons that time in a
halfway house is not the same as incarceration given the
limited “degree of restraint” involved.  Ramsey v. Brennan, 878 F.2d 995, 996 (7th Cir. 1989) (citation omitted);
see U.S. Br. 31-32.
Amicus otherwise resists the practical inquiry by relying on Reno v. Koray, 515 U.S. 50 (1995).  See Br. 32-34,
36-37.  But in Koray, the Court addressed an entirely different question—what constitutes “official detention” for
purposes of crediting the time toward the service of a
prison term under 18 U.S.C. 3585(b), rather than what
constitutes a challenge to custody for purposes of the habeas statute.  515 U.S. at 52.  More broadly, to the extent
that it bears on the inquiry here, Koray undermines amicus’s argument.  The Court there  held that releasing a
pretrial detainee to a corre ctional treatment facility
(which the separate opinions  described as a “halfway
house,” see, e.g., id. at 65 (Ginsburg, J., concurring)), as a
condition of bail was so distinct from imprisonment that it
did not qualify as creditable “detention.”  Id. at 59, 65 (majority opinion).  And the Bureau of Prisons’ guidance that
the Court upheld in Koray specifically determined that
“release” to a halfway house or home confinement “as a
result of [a statute]” or “a condition of bail or bond”—as
opposed to as a matter of the Executive’s discretion—is
not “detention” creditable toward the term of imprisonment.  Id. at 60-61 n.4.
4. In addition, prerelease custody is materially analogous to parole—a status amicus concedes sounds in habeas.  See Pet. Br. 36-37; U. S. Br. 30-32; Amicus Br. 22.
Both federal parole and prerelease custody are programs
run by the Executive Branch that let a prisoner serve a
portion of the end of his sentence outside prison walls,

13

subject to certain restri ctions.  Compare 18 U.S.C.
3624(g), with 18 U.S.C. 4202, 4205, 4209 (1982).  Both are
revocable through non-judicial  proceedings that can return the individual to prison.  Compare 18 U.S.C.
3624(g)(5), with 18 U.S.C. 4214 (1982); 28 C.F.R. 2.52.  And
prerelease custody was one of the two programs that replaced federal parole when Congress enacted the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984.  See Pet. Br. 8.  Amicus is
wrong to treat supervised release as parole’s sole successor.  See Br. 25-26, 28-29.
Amicus purports to devote (B r. 28-34) an entire section of his brief to distinguishing prerelease custody from
parole, yet he says almost nothing about parole itself.  Instead, he points to differences between prerelease custody and supervised release.  For instance, amicus notes
that supervised release takes place after the term of imprisonment (rather than during); it is set by the court at
sentencing (rather than an executive branch official after
the sentencing); and it may be revoked only by a court (rather than an executive branch official).  Br. 30-31.  But in
each respect prerelease custod y is the same as parole.
And even if there are differences between prerelease custody and parole, they are “relatively minor in comparison
to the difference between physical imprisonment and prerelease custody in a halfway house or home confinement.”
U.S. Br. 32; cf. Young v. Harper, 520 U.S. 143, 148-152
(1997) (determining that, despite asserted differences, a
preparole program that entailed release from prison was
equivalent to parole).
5. Amicus ultimately resort s to the practical concern
that any approach other than his own would be “unworkable.”  Br. 34, 36-39.  But that claim hinges on the assumption that Mr. Maxwell’s rule turns on a “fact-intensive” inquiry.  Id. at 36.  As explained above (pp. 9-11), that is incorrect.  The real-world diffe rences between prerelease

14

custody and prison support Mr. Maxwell’s position, but
this Court can readily resolve the issue as a matter of law
because Congress treated prerelease custody as distinct.
Nor has amicus shown how hi s own approach is any
more workable given that it requires courts to consider
whether a claim is sufficiently similar to those in his three
proposed categories.  For instance, amicus asserts that a
claim seeking supervised release falls within the same category as a claim seeking parole.  Br. 24.  But he does not
explain why that is so given the differences between parole and supervised release.  See pp. 12-13, supra.
To the contrary, practical considerations show why
Mr. Maxwell’s claim should sound in habeas.  For one
thing, excluding such claims would potentially leave prisoners wrongly held past their lawful release date with no
remedy at all.  See Pet. Br. 29-32; U.S. Br. 32-34.  Amicus
agrees that the Fifth Circuit “was mistaken” in treating
Bivens as an alternative remedy (Br. 41), but he does not
identify a meaningful alternative.  In particular, amicus
breezily asserts that an implied cause of action would be
available in equity, but he does not grapple with the fact
that this is a notoriously complex area of the law, see Pet.
Br. 31, as the government’s argument (Br. 34) that such a
cause of action would extend only to constitutional claims
well illustrates.  See also William Baude et al., Hart and
Wechsler’s The Federal Courts and the Federal System
1208-1209 (8th ed. 2025).  And amicus cites no authority
for the proposition that ordering the release or transfer of
a prisoner is a type of relief traditionally accorded by
courts of equity.  See Br. 40-41.  Nor does amicus identify
a limiting principle that would avoid inviting a wide range
of prisoner claims to proceed  under an implied cause of
action rather than under carefully circumscribed habeas
doctrine.  In any event, amicus’s theory does not suffice to
defend the judgment below:  if an essentially equivalent

15

vehicle were available to Mr. Maxwell, it was all the more
troubling for the Fifth Circuit to dismiss Mr. Maxwell’s
pro se claim because it was labeled a habeas petition
where the government had not disputed the propriety of
the procedural vehicle and the court could have simply recharacterized the filing as a claim in equity.  See Castro v.
United States , 540 U.S. 375, 381-382 (2003); see also
Haines, 404 U.S. at 520.
Habeas, moreover, is the more sensible avenue for
claims like Mr. Maxwell’s given its substantive and procedural protections for government officials.  See Pet. Br.
32-34; U.S. Br. 34-35.  Amicus dismisses those concerns as
“theoretical” because Congre ss has purportedly barred
all review of such claims brought by federal prisoners under 18 U.S.C. 3621(b).  Br. 42.  But he provides no analysis
in support of that assertion, and it is plainly incorrect.  See
pp. 17-19, infra.  Amicus also whistl es past the burdens
that rejecting habeas could im pose on States, suggesting
(Br. 42) that the Prison Litigation Reform Act provides
them all the protections they need.  But that Act imposes
a “substantially lower gate” than 28 U.S.C. 2254.  Muhammad, 540 U.S. at 751; see U.S. Br. 35.  The consequences of adopting amicus’s proposed approach are particularly stark for the States because his substantial narrowing of the scope of habeas would raise questions about
what other claims by state prisoners could be brought under Section 1983.  In short, amicus’s rule is both legally
and practically unsound, and there is no reason for this
Court to adopt it.
C. The Government’s Alternative Arguments Lack Merit
The government agrees (Br. 24-35, 40) with Mr. Maxwell that the court of appeals erred in resolving the question presented.  In its brief supporting vacatur, the government tosses in a few arguments why, in its view, Mr.

16

Maxwell’s claim “should not ul timately succeed.”  Br. 35.
And, for good measure, it suggests that the Court could
dismiss the writ as improvidently granted.  None of those
arguments provides a basis to do anything other than reverse the judgment below a nd remand for further proceedings.
1. a. The government offers two reasons why, in its
view, affirmance will ultimately be warranted.  The Court
need not address those arguments.  As the government
itself recognizes (Br. 40), the Court’s “usual practice”
would be to “leave matters of  that sort for remand.”
E.M.D. Sales, Inc. v. Carrera, 604 U.S. 45, 54 (2025).  And
the government’s bottom line is that the decision below
should be vacated.  Br. 40, 42; see id. at 1 (styling brief as
“supporting vacatur”).
b. To the extent the Court reaches them, the arguments also lack merit.  As in its brief in opposition, the
government argues (Br. 35-36) that Mr. Maxwell failed to
exhaust his administrative remedies.  But Mr. Maxwell
has multiple arguments for why his pro se filings adequately exhausted his administ rative remedies; any failure to exhaust should be excused; or the district court otherwise erred in dismissing his claim.  See Cert. Reply Br.
2, 8-9.  The court of appeals should address those questions in the first instance.
c. The government then introduces (Br. 36-40) the
argument that 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) bars review of Mr. Maxwell’s habeas claim.
The government admits that it did not raise a Section
3621(b) argument in its brief in opposition; that it dropped
that argument below, raising it in district court but omitting it before the court of appeals; and that the question is
“not ripe for this Court’s re view” because only a single
precedential court of appeals decision has addressed it.

17

Br. 36 n.3, 40.  Especially given the government’s own ambivalence about the argument to date, this Court should
leave it to the court of appea ls to consider it in the first
instance if the government chooses to pursue it on remand.
The government is also plainly wrong that Section
3621(b) bars Mr. Maxwell’s claim.  Section 3621(b) instructs the Bureau of Prisons to “designate the place of
the prisoner’s imprisonment,” and “direct the transfer of
a prisoner from one penal or correctional facility to another” “subject to” various considerations like the resources at a facility, the prox imity to the prisoner’s primary residence, and the prisoner’s characteristics.  18
U.S.C. 3621(b).  It further provides that “[n]otwithstanding any other provision of law, a designation of a place of
imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable by
any court.”  Ibid.; see First Step Act of 2018, § 601, Pub.
L. No. 115-391, 132 Stat. 5237-5238 (adding this language).  The judicial review bar in Section 3621(b) applies
only to the designation of a place of imprisonment “under
this subsection”—meaning Section 3621(b).  Mr. Maxwell’s claim, by contrast, concerns the calculation of
earned-time credits under Section 3624(g), and Section
3632(d)’s unqualified command that the Bureau of Prisons
“shall transfer eligible prisoners, as determined under
section 3624(g), into prerelease custody or supervised release.”  18 U.S.C. 3632(d)(4)(C); see, e.g., Adepoju v.
Scales, 782 F. Supp. 3d 306, 314-315 (E.D. Va. 2025) (collecting cases); see also 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) (imposing a requirement for “making transfers under this subsection”
rather than for all transfers).
Reading the Section 3621(b) limitation to extend to
every subsection also makes no sense in the context of the
statutory scheme:  it is one thing for Congress to prohibit
judicial review over the Bureau of Prisons’ fact-specific

18

assessment of what facility is most appropriate for a prisoner; it is another to create mandatory commands that the
Bureau of Prisons “shall” award earned-time credits and
“shall transfer eligible prisoners” with one hand, while
stripping their enforceability with the other.  See 18
U.S.C. 3624(g)(2), 3632(d)(4)(C);  see also NACDL Br. 7-
12; Raskin Br. 8-12; Senators Br. 11-14.
The government’s contrary interpretation of Section
3621(b) does not withstand scrutiny.  The government
notes (Br. 37) that Section 3621(b) refers to the Bureau of
Prisons’ authority to place a prisoner in a community correctional facility.  But that provision refers to the Bureau’s duty to provide sub stance abuse treatment and
specifies that a sentencing court’s recommendation or request about such placement “shall have no binding effect”
on the Bureau.  18 U.S.C. 3621(b).  That is separate from
the mandatory system of earn ed-time credits and prerelease custody established, in exacting detail, by the First
Step Act.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624(g), 3632(d); see also NACDL
Br. 9-11.  The government also  contends (Br. 37-38) that
the judicial-review bar in Se ction 3621(b) applies to Mr.
Maxwell’s habeas claim based on a series of cross-references and inferences.  But that attenuated chain of reasoning hardly overcomes “both the strong presumption in
favor of judicial review of administrative action and the
longstanding rule requiring a clear statement of congressional intent to repeal habeas jurisdiction.”  INS v. St.
Cyr, 533 U.S. 289, 298 (2001) (footnote omitted).
What is more, a statute wi thdrawing judicial review
over habeas claims in this co ntext would raise significant
constitutional concerns under the Suspension Clause.  See
Samak v. Warden, FCC Coleman-Medium , 766 F.3d
1271, 1291 (11th Cir. 2014) (Pryor, J., concurring) (identifying a “constitutional problem” that arises “when a prisoner seeks to challenge the execution of his sentence, and

19

no court will hear his challenge”).  The government points
out that, at the Founding, habe as courts would not question the validity of a judgment entered by a court of competent jurisdiction.  Br. 39.  But Mr. Maxwell’s claim is
different:  it is that he is be ing imprisoned in a place “expressly forbidden” by statute, like “the hulks of a prison
ship.”  Bonner, 151 U.S. at 256; see Habeas Scholars Br.
12 (explaining that, for centuries, the writ has served “to
conform custody to law”).  An interpretation that avoids
those Suspension Clause questions—namely giving effect
to the “under this subsection” requirement—is at least
“fairly possible.”  Perttu v. Richards, 605 U.S. 460, 468
(2025) (citation omitted).  In the event that the Court
reaches the Section 3621(b) argument, it should therefore
hold that that provision does not bar judicial review here.
2. In its closing paragraph, the government tries to
take a mulligan on its brief in opposition, suggesting that
the Court “may wish to dismis s the writ of certiorari as
improvidently granted.”  Br. 41.  There is no persuasive
reason to dismiss the writ.
The government contends (Br. 41) that the question
“will be essentially academic” if the Court eventually
holds that Section 3621(b) bars judicial review.  But, as
just explained, the Section 3621(b) judicial review bar
does not apply.  In any event, the Court routinely resolves
questions despite the possibility that subsequent developments could deprive its ruling of practical significance.
See, e.g., Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy, 601 U.S.
366, 371 (2024); see also Chatrie v. United States, 609 U.S.
605, 614 n.2 (2026); id. at 656-657 (Alito, J., dissenting).  As
the government itself recognizes, moreover, the availability of level-of-custody claims in habeas has ongoing practical significance beyond this particular provision of the
First Step Act, including for state prisoners.  See Br. 41.

20

The government also gestures (Br. 41) at the possibility that “this case may beco me moot in a matter of
months” because the Bureau of Prisons “projects” that
Mr. Maxwell will be transferred to prerelease custody in
January 2027.  The government did not note that timing
when it submitted its brief in opposition, and this Court
has emphasized that “post-certiorari actions that would
insulate a decision from review  *   *   *  must be viewed
with a critical eye.”  West Virginia v. B. P. J. , 146 S. Ct.
2356, 2373 n.3 (2026) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).  Cf. S. Ct. R. 36 (requiring leave of court to
transfer a habeas petitioner pending this Court’s review).
There is also reason to be skeptical of the Bureau’s “project[ion]” given that it appears that Mr. Maxwell has received multiple notices sugge sting various release dates
for his transfer to a halfway house, which each time have
been withdrawn or modified.
The Court can avoid any ques tion of mootness by deciding this straightforward case promptly after argument.
And if Mr. Maxwell is released before the Court issues an
opinion, this Court can reverse the court of appeals’ decision dismissing on a threshold ground before addressing
any question of mootness.  See, e.g., Sinochem International Co. v. Malaysia International Shipping Corp., 549
U.S. 422, 431 (2007).
In any event, after release,  Mr. Maxwell will still retain “a legally cognizable interest in the outcome.”  Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013) (citation
omitted).  That is because Mr. Maxwell would rely on a
judicial order restoring his earned-time credits to reduce
his overall time in supervised release.  See  Gonzalez v.
Herrera, 151 F.4th 1076, 1079-1080 (9th Cir. 2025); see
also Rivera-Perez v. Flowers, No. 26-396 (cert. petition
filed Sept. 17, 2026).  The government appears to disagree
that earned-time credits can be used for that purpose,

21

Gonzalez, 151 F.4th at 1078, but that disagreement would
concern the merits of the dispute, not mootness.  See, e.g.,
Chafin v. Chafin, 568 U.S. 165, 174 (2013).  In addition,
the government has offered nothing to meet its “formidable burden of showing that it is absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected
to recur.”  Already, 568 U.S. at 91 (citation omitted).  In
short, there is no obstacle to resolving the question presented.  The Court should an swer that question and reverse the judgment below.
